title: Morning Robotics Scan
report:
## Hyundai Elevator Miri API

### The Breakthrough
Hyundai Elevator unveiled its cloud‑based Miri API that lets robots request, ride, and exit elevators without any physical call buttons. The API translates robot floor‑request messages into elevator control commands and is already active on about 91 elevators, serving over 70 robots across hospitals and delivery sites. This eliminates retrofitting and enables seamless vertical mobility for embodied AI fleets.

### The Caveats
The claim rests on anecdotal deployments with no quantitative performance or safety validation, so its real reliability remains unproven.

## Data‑efficient Neural Imitation of MPC

### The Breakthrough
The authors introduced Self‑Informed Sampling (SIFS) to train neural networks that imitate long‑horizon, non‑convex time‑optimal MPC with hard terminal constraints. By learning a time‑to‑go signal, SIFS queries the expert only where the policy deviates, cutting training time to about one‑third and data use to less than half. On a Furuta pendulum the resulting neural controller runs at 1 kHz—over 700× faster than the expert—while preserving the expert’s region of attraction.

### The Caveats
The approach is demonstrated only on a single Furuta pendulum, so its data‑efficiency and real‑time performance on higher‑dimensional or different robotic tasks remain unproven.

## UAV‑Flow++ Benchmark

### The Breakthrough
UAV‑Flow++ provides a suite of >30 k real and 10 k simulated UAV trajectories paired with natural‑language commands, defining the Flow task for short‑range, object‑relative flight. The authors pretrained a policy (FlowVLA) via mixed imitation and refined it with Tail‑Aware GRPO, achieving 93.16% success—a 6.72‑point gain over the strongest unnamed baseline—in simulation and real‑world tests. This creates a new benchmark for language‑guided UAV maneuvering and demonstrates strong sample efficiency.

### The Caveats
The reported 6.72‑point gain is against an unnamed baseline, so it’s unclear how the method compares to existing state‑of‑the‑art approaches.

## FORGE Humanoid Control

### The Breakthrough
FORGE introduces a coarse‑to‑fine command hierarchy combined with a momentum observer to estimate low‑frequency wrist‑equivalent forces from proprioception, enabling a humanoid to walk, balance, and manipulate with only sparse wrist pose commands and optional force inputs. The system fuses locomotion priors with quasi‑static virtual‑target loops, allowing whole‑body corrections without joint‑angle references. This could simplify teleoperated data collection and improve robustness in complex loco‑manipulation tasks.

### The Caveats
The paper reports only simulated results and names no existing controller baselines, so its claimed precision and stability for humanoid loco‑manipulation remain unsubstantiated.

## Periodic‑Oriented Programming (POP)

### The Breakthrough
POP proposes keeping all robot logic inside the 50 Hz periodic loops, centralizing control decisions in robotPeriodic or subsystem periodic methods so hardware is touched exactly once per tick. Subsystems expose high‑level set‑point APIs while the periodic function enforces safety constraints, logs telemetry, and reduces state, encouraging combined subsystems where logic intertwines. This design aims to produce safer, easier‑to‑debug FRC code.

### The Caveats
The claim that POP yields simpler, more reliable code is unsupported, as the post provides no empirical comparison to existing command‑based frameworks or any real‑world trial data.

## WendyOS Deployment OS

### The Breakthrough
WendyOS bundles a lightweight Linux distro, a Wendy agent, and a CLI that automates container builds, USB‑C discovery, and OTA rollbacks, enabling one‑click deployment of containerised apps to physical or virtual robots without cloud‑based CI/CD. The tutorial demonstrates a full edit‑re‑deploy loop in under a minute on a generic robot board, supporting both real hardware via USB‑C and QEMU‑based virtual robots with identical workflow.

### The Caveats
The demo never validates the workflow on actual robot hardware, so its claimed benefits over existing robot‑OS deployment tools remain unproven.

## Skamandros Tenstorrent Driver

### The Breakthrough
Skamandros delivers a 1 MB driver and compiler for Tenstorrent AI chips, offering a PTX‑like front‑end that translates high‑level kernels into device‑specific instructions with automatic tiling and operation fusion. By bundling driver and compiler, it removes the need for proprietary toolchains and enables direct programming of the p100a card on edge hardware.

### The Caveats
The demo offers no performance benchmarks or comparisons to existing toolchains and is demonstrated only on a single p100a kernel, leaving its practicality for real AI workloads and other Tenstorrent devices unproven.

## Spirula Studio 3D Reconstruction

### The Breakthrough
Spirula Studio is a self‑contained C++ binary that trains 3D Gaussian Splatting models from raw photos or video, running on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs via Vulkan (or CUDA) without requiring Python, PyTorch, or COLMAP. It fits up to 10 million SH3 Gaussians in 8 GB VRAM using quantised training and includes a fast Structure‑from‑Motion module and AI‑based masking for high‑quality textured meshes.

### The Caveats
The repository provides no quantitative comparison to existing 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines, so the claimed speed and quality improvements are unverified.

## Cadence Equilibrium Network

### The Breakthrough
Cadence implements a brain‑inspired equilibrium network where a graph of rate neurons settles to produce actions, and learning occurs locally from the delta between successive equilibria, eliminating back‑propagation. It ships with demos ranging from robot arms to Atari games, offering System 1 for fast perception‑action loops and optional System 2 for slower corrective updates via a simple Python API.

### The Caveats
The repository offers no quantitative benchmarks or baseline comparisons, so it’s unclear whether its equilibrium‑learning approach actually matches or exceeds existing online learning methods.

## ProtoVis‑Nav Visual Imagination

### The Breakthrough
ProtoVis‑Nav equips a UAV navigation model with a visual imagination module that predicts a set of feature prototypes for the intended next region and linearly combines them to generate an imagined visual representation. This imagined context is fed to the VLN policy, yielding substantially higher waypoint accuracy on UAV visual‑language navigation tasks.

### The Caveats
The paper claims substantial gains but does not name any VLN baselines for comparison, leaving the reported improvement unverifiable.

### Priority
Hyundai’s Miri API is the most impactful story today because it demonstrates a concrete, cloud‑based solution that already enables dozens of robots to move vertically in real buildings—a capability that unlocks new use‑cases for embodied AI.

### One action
Consider evaluating the Miri API for any indoor robot fleet you manage or prototype, focusing on the API’s floor‑request messages to integrate elevator navigation without hardware retrofits.

### What to watch
UAV‑Flow++ and ProtoVis‑Nav both push language‑guided drone flight forward, but Flow++ emphasizes large‑scale data collection and a reinforced policy that already succeeds in real flights, while ProtoVis‑Nav adds a visual imagination layer to improve waypoint precision. Watching how these approaches combine—large datasets with imagined visual context—could shape the next generation of robust UAV navigation systems.
